summary:
Ember Atlas is an AI-assisted fire-safety dashboard built on NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion archive. NASA's data is scattered across 21 experiment tables, each with its own columns and units. We merged them into one dataset: 23 investigations, 1,730 test runs and 286 test conditions.

Users pick a mission atmosphere (ISS, lunar habitat, pressurized rover, Mars or spacesuit), or set oxygen, pressure and airflow themselves. Ember Atlas then ranks every investigation by how closely its test conditions match, how relevant it is to the mission and how strong its evidence is. An interactive atmosphere map plots every run and reveals a critical gap: solid materials have only been burned in microgravity up to about 22% oxygen, while planned habitats will run at 30–34%. A Gemini-powered analyst writes briefings that cite the investigations behind each answer. A 3D Flame Lab wind tunnel lets anyone burn cotton, Nomex or PMMA under orbital, lunar or Martian conditions, using a burn model checked against Saffire-II measurements.

Without gravity, flames spread and die in ways Earth tests don't predict. Ember Atlas turns terabytes of scattered data into clear, cited answers for the people designing safe homes on the Moon and Mars.
details:
What it does

Ember Atlas is a fire-safety dashboard built on NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion archive. You pick where a crew will live (the ISS, a lunar surface habitat, a pressurized rover, a Mars habitat or a spacesuit), or set oxygen, pressure and airflow yourself. Ember Atlas then ranks all 23 PSI combustion investigations by how relevant they are to that atmosphere and shows where the evidence runs out.

How it works

1. Data pipeline: a Python script downloads the investigation records and 21 experiment tables through the public PSI API. Each table uses its own column names and units, so we wrote a normalizer that converts them into one schema (oxygen %, pressure, airflow, fuel, phase, outcome, burn rate), runs sanity checks and fixes obvious errors. The result is 1,730 test runs and 286 test conditions.

2. Ranking: each investigation is scored 35% on how closely its tested conditions match, 25% on mission fit, 20% on relevance and 20% on strength of evidence. Users can change the mission priorities.

3. Atmosphere map: every run is plotted by oxygen and pressure, with each habitat marked. It reveals a key gap: no solid material has burned above 22.2% oxygen in PSI flight data, yet lunar habitats and rovers are planned at 30–34%.

4. AI analyst: a Google Gemini model, given only the top-ranked PSI records, writes briefings that cite the investigation behind each claim and say plainly where data is missing. Briefings download as Markdown.

5. Flame Lab: a 3D wind tunnel where users burn cotton, Nomex, PMMA, silicone and other materials under orbital, lunar or Martian oxygen, pressure, airflow and gravity. Its simplified burn model was checked against Saffire-II's measured spread rates of 2.1–2.6 mm/s.

Also included: a network of related studies, side-by-side comparison, Earth spinoffs, CSV export and shareable links that save the exact view.

Benefits and impact

Engineers, researchers and students get answers in seconds instead of digging through terabytes of scattered tables. Most importantly, Ember Atlas shows where NASA should test next: materials like Nomex that self-extinguish in Earth air can keep burning at the oxygen levels planned for the Moon.

Tools and technologies

Next.js 15, React 19 and TypeScript; three.js and a hand-written WebGL shader; custom SVG charts; Python for the data pipeline; Google Gemini API; hosted on Vercel with code on GitHub. Data: NASA PSI (CC0).

What makes it creative

It turns a spreadsheet archive into something you can feel: a flame on the landing page that changes shape as you scroll away from Earth, mission-style dials, and a wind tunnel where you watch a material ignite or go out.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty: every AI claim is cited, every assumed value is flagged, and the Flame Lab is labelled a teaching model, not a NASA simulation. Also accessibility and mobile use, keeping the AI key on the server, and no NASA logos or branding.
